How this book matches your exam. Research check: this book follows the Cambridge International AS & A Level English Language 9093 syllabus (the current syllabus runs until a revised version is examined from 2029).

This book prepares you for Paper 1 Section B: analysing how form, structure and language create meaning and effect in an unseen text (about 550–750 words), worth 25 marks. Answers are marked with levels, mainly for AO1 (reading and understanding) and AO3 (analysing form, structure and language). The model texts in this book are original, written for practice. Our mark guides describe what earns credit; they are not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: What Paper 1 Section B Asks For

Key ideas

  • The task: "Analyse the text, focusing on form, structure and language." The text may be non-fiction (article, speech, travel writing, blog, advertisement, memoir) or literary non-fiction.
  • Marks (25): reward understanding of the text's purpose and audience, and analysis of how specific choices create meaning and effects.
  • Higher-level answers: precise terminology, embedded short quotations, explanation of effect on the reader linked to purpose, overview of the whole text, and coverage of form, structure and language.
  • Time: about 60 minutes (the paper is 2 h 15 min for two 25-mark sections), including 10 minutes reading and planning.

Worked examples

Example 1 (weak): "The writer uses lots of adjectives to make it interesting."

Example 2 (better): "The adjectives 'cramped' and 'airless' build a semantic field of confinement, making the reader share the narrator's growing panic."

Example 3 (overview): "This travel blog aims to entertain and persuade younger readers to visit, moving from comic frustration to awe."

10-mark exam-style task

Read this opening of a blog post:

"Nobody warns you about the stairs. Two hundred and eighty-seven of them, slick with last night's rain, winding up the hill like a question nobody wants to answer. I counted every one. By step ninety my legs had filed a formal complaint."

(a) Identify the likely audience and purpose. [2]

(b) Analyse two language features and their effects. [6]

(c) Comment on one structural feature of the extract. [2]

Answers and mark guide:

  • (a) Readers of a travel/lifestyle blog, probably young adults (B1); to entertain while recounting a travel experience (B1).
  • (b) For each feature (B1 identify + B1 quotation + B1 effect): the simile "like a question nobody wants to answer" personifies the staircase as something daunting and unresolved, creating humour and suspense; personification/hyperbole "my legs had filed a formal complaint" uses bureaucratic lexis comically, building a self-deprecating, relatable voice; the precise number "Two hundred and eighty-seven" stresses the ordeal.
  • (c) The short declarative opening "Nobody warns you about the stairs." hooks the reader with direct address and a confiding tone (B1), before the longer sentence expands on the challenge (B1).

Common mistakes

  1. Feature-spotting without explaining effects.
  2. Long quotations instead of short embedded ones.
  3. Ignoring structure and form.
  4. Generic effects ("it makes the reader want to read on").
  5. No overview of purpose and audience.

Quick recall

  1. Three areas to analyse?
  2. Marks for Section B?
  3. Length of the unseen text?
  4. What do higher levels need?
  5. Suggested time for Section B?

Answers: 1) Form, structure, language. 2) 25. 3) About 550–750 words. 4) Precise terminology, embedded quotations and developed effects linked to purpose. 5) About 60 minutes.
